(1) IWUAs are the key to success of irrigation projects; (2) IWUAs must be organized, not imposed from above; (3) the IWUA must be supported by the state and other stakeholders; (4) IWUAs should be supported to develop their own capacity and leadership; (5) the state should provide a legal and regulatory framework for IWUAs to operate; (6) the state should not be the sole provider of services; and (7

the most successful IWUAs are those that are: (a) formed in a participatory and inclusive process; (b) have strong leadership and management; (c) are supported with adequate financial, technical and human resources; (d) have clear and well-defined rules; and (e) have effective and transparent systems for monitoring and enforcing rules.

the following questions: (i) what is the role of the IWUA and how does it relate to other institutions?;
understanding how to create, support and strengthen the IWUA as the key institution for managing irrigation schemes.

the success of an irrigation program depends on a strong IWUA, and that a strong IWUA is created by following a systematic process.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IWUAs are not the solution to the problems of irrigation, but they can be a part of the solution, and that the key to their success is to invest in them as much as in the hardware.

the most important lesson learned is that the success of a communal irrigation program depends on a strong and effective irrigation organization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the process for creating an effective and inclusive IWUA is not a simple one.
the success of IWUAs is not a function of the organizational design of the IWUA, but rather the quality of the process of organizing the IWUA.
there are no shortcuts to success.
